summary: Specifies the IPv6 Flow Label field and the minimum requirements for source nodes that label flows, nodes that forward labeled packets, and flow state establishment methods. The field makes flow classification possible from main header fields in fixed positions. It is a proposed standard that has been replaced by RFC 6437.

plainLanguage.summary: Each IPv6 packet has a tag showing which conversation it belongs to, like a color wristband for friends. Routers can sort packets by the tag without opening them. RFC 6437 replaced it.

subtitle: A 20-bit tag for identifying flows and enabling efficient packet classification.

tldr.problem: Routers need to classify packets belonging to the same flow without examining transport layer headers, which may be unavailable due to fragmentation or encryption.
tldr.mechanism: The IPv6 Flow Label field provides a 20-bit tag that, combined with source and destination addresses, uniquely identifies a flow. Source nodes label packets belonging to the same flow with the same value, and routers use this 3-tuple for efficient classification.
tldr.outcome: Routers can perform flow-specific processing without needing to parse nested headers. RFC 6437 superseded this with updated requirements.

today: RFC 3697 is a Proposed Standard that has been superseded by RFC 6437, which updates the flow label specification.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
A flow is a sequence of packets sent from a source to a destination that the sender marks with the same label. It might be a TCP connection, a media stream, or any group of related packets. Traditionally, routers classify flows using a 5-tuple: source address, destination address, source port, destination port, and protocol type. However, this approach fails when transport headers are encrypted or when packets are fragmented, and it requires routers to examine deep into the packet structure.

The IPv6 Flow Label field provides a simpler solution. The RFC specifies that a 20-bit value in the IPv6 header, combined with the source and destination addresses (a 3-tuple), uniquely identifies a flow. This allows routers to classify packets by reading only the fixed-position main IPv6 header fields, making flow-specific processing much more efficient.
sections.plainLanguage: Routers need to sort packets into conversations. The flow label is a sticker that says which conversation a packet belongs to. Routers can see the sticker without opening the packet.

sections.title: The Flow Label Field
sections.content:
The Flow Label occupies a 20-bit field in the IPv6 header. A value of zero indicates that the packet is not part of any labeled flow. The source node assigns the label and must deliver the same value unchanged to the destination. Routers MUST NOT assume any mathematical properties of the Flow Label values; they may be sequential, random, or anything else. A poor hash function based solely on Flow Label bits can degrade router performance.

Nodes keeping flow state (such as routers performing QoS processing) must forget flow state if no packet from that flow arrives for 120 seconds or more, unless a specific flow state establishment method defines a longer lifetime. The Flow Label does not mandate any particular packet reordering policy.
sections.plainLanguage: The label is a 20-bit number. Zero means no label. The sender chooses the number, and it goes all the way to the receiver unchanged.

sections.title: Flow Labeling Requirements
sections.content:
Source nodes SHOULD assign a new Flow Label to each unrelated transport connection or application data stream, even if the node itself does not require flow-specific treatment. This enables receiver-oriented resource reservations and load spreading across intermediate nodes. Nodes that do not assign traffic to flows MUST set the Flow Label to zero.

To prevent accidental reuse, a source node MUST NOT assign a Flow Label value it recently used with the same source-destination address pair within 120 seconds of the previous flow's termination. The RFC recommends selecting new labels in a well-defined sequence (sequential or pseudo-random) and initializing the starting value from non-volatile memory or a cryptographically sound random source on each system restart.
sections.plainLanguage: When you send a new conversation, pick a new number that you haven't used with the same address pair recently. This prevents mix-ups.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Since flows are identified by a 3-tuple including source and destination addresses, the security risks of the Flow Label are closely related to address spoofing attacks. An attacker who can forge an address can likely forge a label, and vice versa. An attacker might obtain better service by modifying the Flow Label or injecting packets with false labels and addresses; such theft-of-service can escalate to denial-of-service by depleting resources.

With ingress filtering in place, most full 3-tuple forgeries become difficult, limiting the risk to attacks that modify a Flow Label on a correctly addressed packet. Only applications with appropriate privilege can set non-zero Flow Labels. IPsec tunnel mode protects the inner header's Flow Label; however, IPsec does not protect the Flow Label in the outer header, so a man-in-the-middle can still modify it without affecting IPsec integrity checks.
sections.plainLanguage: Someone could fake the sticker to get unfair treatment. Firewalls that check who the packet is really from help stop this.

sections.title: Flow State Establishment
sections.content:
The RFC does not specify how routers establish flow state or what treatment flows receive; those are left to separate standards. Instead, it defines only the generic requirements any such method must meet. Flow state establishment methods MUST provide a way for routers to clean up state when a flow ends. They MUST also be able to recover if the requested flow state cannot be supported by a router.

To enable coexistence of different flow establishment methods in the same IPv6 nodes, these basic requirements ensure that no single method locks out others and that systems degrade gracefully if resources are exhausted.
sections.plainLanguage: Different ways to set up special handling for flows can coexist as long as they clean up after themselves and don't crash if the router runs out of space.
